newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil income inequalities persist under Real Plan.
newsitem.headline: Brazil income inequalities persist under Real Plan.

text.p: Brazilian income distribution is still highly inequitable despite the government's anti-inflation Real Plan which has reduced poverty since its introduction in July 1994, economic researchers said Wednesday.

Brazil's inflation has been reduced to 10 percent a year from about 5000 percent before the Real Plan, and the government of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso says 13 million Brazilians have risen above the poverty line as a result of the stabilized economy.

"Poverty is one thing, unequal income distribution another," said Marcelo Neri, researcher with the government's Applied Economics Research Institute (Ipea). "The cake is bigger, but it's distributed even worse."
Shortly before the onset of the Real Plan, recorded Brazilian income distribution had reached a zenith of inequality, Neri said.
In May 1994, he said, the richest 10 percent of Brazilians earned 7.61 times more than the poorest 40 percent.

By 1996, the richest 10 percent earned only 6.38 times as much, but this figure is still worse than in 1992 when the richest 10 percent earned only 5.35 times as much as the poorest 40 percent. Meanwhile, Brazilian per capita income increased 28 percent between 1992 and 1996.

"Ending inflation is more like a necessary condition than a sufficient measure to improve the inequalities of income distribution," Neri said. "Low inflation allows the government to carry out policies which reduce unequal distribution."

Cardoso conceived of the Real Plan when he was finance minister in the previous government of President Itamar Franco. It introduced a new currency, the real, which was tied loosely to the dollar, and did away with automatic monthly wage and price increases which for years fueled inflation.
Neri said the sharpest improvement in income distribution since the Real Plan coincided with a 43 percent minimum salary increase in May 1995, but since then there was no strong ameloriating trend.

A recent study by Ipea researchers Ricardo Paes de Barros and Rosane Mendonca concluded that education was the key to Brazil's inequalities of wealth, rather than inflation, race, gender or regional differences.
They found that even more so than increasing funding, education ought to be decentralized to become more efficient by allowing individual schools to adapt to the particular needs of their students.
Barros and Mendonca also concluded that the quality of education in public and private schools had to be comparable to ensure equal access to universities for the rich and poor.

Neri said even though Brazil had one of the most unequal if not the most inequitable income distribution in the world there was a huge potential for eliminating poverty if the government introduced the appropriate policies.

"Brazil is not a poor country. Brazilian's earn more per capita than 75 percent of the world's population," Neri said. "Solving the poverty problem in Brazil would be easier than in India, for example, where there is simply no income to distribute."
